title: What Should a Pastor Do in the First Ninety Days?
subtitle: A new pastor's guide to the first three months in a church, why listening matters more than leading at the start, the mistakes that wound a ministry before it begins, and how to build the trust everything else will depend on.

sections.title: You Will Want to Lead Immediately
sections.body:
You arrive with energy and ideas and a sense of calling, and the temptation of the first ninety days is to start leading on day one. Resist it with everything you have.

The new pastor sees the problems quickly. The worship is dated, the systems are broken, the board meets too long and decides too little. All of it is probably true. And almost none of it should be touched in the first three months, because you do not yet have the one thing that gives you the right to change anything. You do not have trust, and trust is the currency every reform will be paid for in.

I moved too fast in my first church. I saw what needed fixing and I fixed it, and I could not understand why people who agreed the thing was broken resented me for repairing it. It took years to learn what those months cost me. They did not resent the change. They resented being changed by a stranger who had not yet earned the standing to touch what they loved.

Be quick to hear and slow to speak, James wrote, and there is no season where that verse matters more than the one you are about to enter. You were called to lead this church. You will lead it for years. You do not have to lead it on Tuesday.

sections.title: Listen Until It Is Uncomfortable
sections.body:
The first work of a new pastor is not preaching, though you will preach. It is not vision, though vision will come. The first work is listening, and most of us are terrible at it because we mistake it for waiting to talk.

Real listening in a new church means asking the old members to tell you the story of this place and then actually receiving it. What has God done here. Who are the saints who built this. What are the wounds, the splits, the seasons of glory, the names spoken with reverence and the names spoken carefully. Every church is a living history, and the pastor who does not learn it will keep stepping on graves he did not know were there.

Listen until it is uncomfortable, until you have heard the same story from enough angles to know where the bodies are buried and where the treasure is hidden. Listen to the critics and the cheerleaders, the long-timers and the newcomers, the staff and the people who left. He who answers before listening, the proverb says, that is his folly and his shame. The new pastor who speaks before he has listened is building his whole ministry on a foundation he never inspected.

This is not passivity. It is the most active and strategic thing you will do all year. You are learning the church well enough to one day lead it somewhere it will actually follow.

sections.title: Be a Pastor Before You Are a Reformer
sections.body:
There is a question every new congregation is asking that they will never put into words. Does this man love us, or does he love what he can make of us. They are watching to find out, and they will know the answer before you do.

The pastor who arrives as a reformer signals the second answer. He came to fix them. He sees a project, not a people, and a flock can smell that from the back row. But the pastor who shows up at the hospital, who learns the children's names, who sits with the dying widow and weeps at the funeral of a man he barely met, he answers the first question with his body. He loves them. And love buys a hearing that strategy never could.

Jesus had compassion on the crowds because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. The compassion came first. The teaching followed. The order is not decorative. People do not open their lives to a leader they suspect is using them, and they open everything to one they are convinced loves them.

Do the funerals. Do the hospital visits. Learn the names. Be a pastor first and a reformer later, because the love you build in these months is the only thing strong enough to carry the changes that have to come after. Skip this and every later reform is built on sand.

sections.title: The Wounds You Inflict Without Meaning To
sections.body:
Some mistakes in the first ninety days do not heal. They scar, and the scar shapes everything after. Know them so you can refuse them.

Do not criticize your predecessor, even gently, even when invited, even when the criticism is fair and the people seem to want it. The moment you diminish the one before you, every person who loved him learns that you are a man who diminishes, and they file it away against the day it might be them. Honor the work that came before, including its flaws, because grace toward your predecessor is grace they are watching you practice for their own future.

Do not pick an early fight to establish authority. Authority established by force in the first season is authority you will have to keep re-establishing by force forever. Do not move the furniture, change the order of service, or rewrite the sacred cows before you understand why they are sacred. And do not promise. The new pastor wanting to be loved makes promises in month two that he cannot keep in year two, and a broken promise early teaches the church that your word is provisional.

Let your yes be yes. Make few commitments and keep all of them. The ministry you are building will rest on whether your people learned, in these first months, that you are a man whose words can be trusted.

sections.title: You Are Pouring a Foundation
sections.body:
Here is what the first ninety days actually are, and if you understand it you will treat them differently. You are not leading yet. You are pouring a foundation, and a foundation is invisible the moment the building goes up, and the building falls without it.

Nothing you do in these months will look impressive. No bold vision launched, no problem solved, no program built. You will feel, some days, like you are not earning your salary, like a real leader would be doing more. That feeling is a liar. The unglamorous work of listening and loving and learning is the most important leadership you will ever do in this church, precisely because it is the work no one applauds and everyone depends on.

By wisdom a house is built, the proverb says, and by understanding it is established. Understanding comes before establishment. You cannot skip to the part where you lead boldly. The boldness has to stand on something, and the something is the trust you are quietly accumulating now, in a thousand small faithful acts that no one will remember and everyone will rely on.

Go slow. Listen long. Love first. Pour the foundation deep and true in these ninety days, and then spend the years that follow building something on top of it that lasts. The church you can lead in year five is being decided right now, in the months when it looks like you are barely leading at all.
